writeup.headline: 59 renovation permits lead the city in Ward 1, where time poverty ranks worst of the 50.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Two of the ward's strongest scores lean on the same method. Both come from census figures reported at the tract level and then reassigned to ward boundaries, so wherever a tract crosses into a neighboring ward, part of what gets attributed to Ward 1 may really belong next door. On the environmental justice share, seventeen wards score close enough that two points covers the lot of them, and the publisher marks that number low confidence. On the related industrial-site proximity index, twenty seven wards sit near enough that a two point spread would take in every one of them, and half of Chicago's fifty wards fall inside an eleven point range on that same index, so the first place finish is a thinner lead than it looks.

The ward's perfect participatory budgeting score, which comes from letting residents vote on how their menu dollars get spent, is far from a lonely lead. Thirteen wards cluster close enough behind it that two points would swallow the whole group, and the underlying number reflects a ward map redrawn in 2023, so it describes today's footprint rather than whatever shape came before it. Nobody actually counted the figure that puts this ward last on modeled time poverty. It is built by matching national time-use survey results to the ward's population profile, and the publisher rates the estimate low confidence, meaning it says more about a typically built ward like this one than about any single resident's real week.
writeup.summary:
Logan Square, West Town, and part of the Near West Side sit inside Ward 1, good for a 63.48 score and 4th place citywide this year. Nightlife and home improvement drive its strongest marks. Thirty six coffee shops and thirty bars here carry top ratings, more of either kind than turns up anywhere else in the fifty, and 59 home renovation permits went out in a single year, also the most citywide. On the environmental side, the share of residents living inside a flagged environmental justice zone reads close to zero here, and a separate distance-weighted score puts this ward farther from major industrial risk sites than the other forty nine, both good for first place.

Free time is where the numbers turn. Residents here are modeled as more time-strapped than all but one of Chicago's other wards, and separate estimates put weekly religious attendance and the strength of religious affiliation both among the lowest scores in the fifty. A modeled depression measure lands in similar territory, and parking runs tight too, with the ward's block-face density trailing most of the city. Put another way, this is a packed, amenity-rich stretch of Chicago where the data paints residents as busy and stretched thin, even while crediting the ward with heavy renovation activity and clean environmental scores.

writeup.headline: Fast 311 turnaround and the worst air quality scores in Chicago both show up in Ward 2.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
The menu-budget figure comes straight from the source, but sixteen other wards sit close enough to it that a two point window would fold in the rest of the pack. Because Chicago redrew ward boundaries in 2023, the number also reflects today's shape rather than whatever the ward looked like under the old map.

Short commutes get measured the same way, by spreading census tract figures across the ward, so a slice of what gets counted toward Ward 2 may actually sit across the line in a neighboring ward. The publisher marks that figure medium confidence. The worst-in-Chicago mark on air-toxics hazard rests on the identical tract math and carries the same medium-confidence label, so the ranking is real but drawn with less precision than a single number suggests.
writeup.summary:
Lincoln Park and the Near North Side make up most of Ward 2's footprint. It sits 11th among the city's 50 wards, scoring 54.83. Municipal response speed stands out most. Crews here clear tree-debris 311 requests faster than the rest of the fifty, and the ward put its full menu allotment, close to $1.5 million a year, entirely into projects, the top mark in the city. Commute times run short too, with fewer workers logging 45-plus-minute trips than in nearly every other part of Chicago, and a modeled favor-trading measure between neighbors also tops the list here.

Two pollution measures land the ward at the bottom of Chicago, one an air-toxics hazard index, the other a modeled cancer-risk figure built from those same pollutants. Living alone is common here too. Just under six in ten households hold a single resident, the highest rate anywhere in the fifty, and the ward posts the lowest child-care center availability score along with a near-last mark on winter sunlight reaching street level. Add it up and this is a ward built for speed and density, strong on basic services, weak on air, solo households, and sunlight.

writeup.headline: Washington Park and Grand Boulevard give Ward 3 deep history and a tough rental market.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Two of these rankings need a second look beyond the raw number. The ward's National Register count places 2nd, but that 2nd place is measured against just 41 wards with usable data, not the complete set of fifty, so it is a high mark within a partial field, not a clean sweep of the whole city.

That leaves the landlord-profit numbers, which land the ward 47th out of 50. Eleven wards score close enough on this same measure that two points would gather in the entire group, so the bottom of this ranking is a crowd, not a clean last-place gap. A separate figure, how evenly the ward's yearly menu budget reaches its own blocks rather than clustering in one corner, ties back to boundaries that shifted in the 2023 redraw, so part of the historical trend behind that number reflects a ward that no longer exists in its old shape.
writeup.summary:
Ward 3 stretches across Douglas, Washington Park, Grand Boulevard, and the Near South Side. Its 44.67 score lands it 29th of 50, squarely in the middle of the pack. Preservation and city responsiveness carry the ward's best marks. Thirty one properties here made it onto the National Register of Historic Places, while a separate 35 hold official Chicago Landmark status, both counts running higher than most of the fifty, and 33 mapped parks put the ward in third place on green space. City crews respond quickly too, with rodent-baiting calls closing in just under three days and street-light repairs wrapped up in well under two, another top-three turnaround time in Chicago.

Housing tells a different story. Eighty five percent of residential parcels here list a taxpayer address that does not match the property itself, the largest share among Chicago's fifty wards, a strong signal of landlord and investor ownership rather than owner-occupancy. A separate estimate finds landlords keeping roughly 70 cents of every rent dollar collected here as profit rather than mortgage payoff, a mark that trails most of the city. The ward's houses of worship also span a narrower range of religious traditions than most other wards. Put together, Ward 3 carries one of the city's stronger preservation and civic records inside a housing market that leans heavily toward landlords.

writeup.headline: Landmark density in Ward 4 leads the city, while school attendance and retail lag behind.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
This ward's landmark tally reads as commanding at first place, but half of Chicago's fifty wards land inside just a six point band on this measure, so most wards actually cluster close together and being first here is not the same as running away from the field.

Second place on menu budget use, meaning the share of last year's roughly $1.5 million capital allotment that actually got spent rather than left on the table, carries a similar catch. Sixteen wards trail this score by less than two points, so the runner-up spot sits closer to a crowd than to a clean lead, and the figures behind it predate, in part, the 2023 line redraw, so some of what built this number came from a ward whose shape no longer matches today's. The congregation count per 10,000 residents, also 2nd place, comes from ZIP code totals that ignore ward lines entirely, and the publisher rates that figure low confidence too.
writeup.summary:
Oakland, Kenwood, Douglas, and the Near South Side make up Ward 4. A 49.76 score puts it 17th among Chicago's 50 wards this year. History and geography set this ward apart. Landmark counts here run higher than anywhere else in Chicago, 130 in all, alongside 212 separately counted sites spanning civic, cultural, and public uses, also tops in the city. A separate historic-building survey conducted between 1983 and 1995 counted 755 significant pre-1940 structures here, the second-highest total in the fifty. Residents here live roughly 0.7 miles from the Lake Michigan shoreline, and only one ward sits closer to the water. The ward also came in 2nd on committing its full annual menu allotment to projects.

Retail and school numbers pull the other direction. Independent grocers and restaurants are scarce by comparison. Roughly six in ten of the food stores licensed to operate here sell through a chain rather than an independent owner, and national chains alone, the 100 largest by size, account for close to 21 percent, both figures on the high end citywide. Nearly half the students at schools serving this ward miss a tenth or more of the school year. The ward's own capital dollars also land unevenly across its blocks rather than spreading citywide. Ward 4 ends up an odd pairing, among the most landmark-dense wards in Chicago, but with a retail scene leaning heavily toward chains and attendance numbers trailing much of the rest of the city.

writeup.reading_the_rankings:
The top mark here on modeled cancer risk from air toxics reads well at first glance, but it comes from spreading census tract figures across today's ward map, so wherever a tract spans two wards, part of what lands here could really belong on the far side of that line. Confidence in that number sits at medium, per the publisher.

It counts how often the council seat was filled rather than anything happening on the ground here, so it describes an office and not a neighbourhood. Ward boundaries also changed in the 2023 redraw, which means the figure mixes whoever held that seat before and after the map moved rather than tracking one uninterrupted term.

The bottom spot for money invested in new residential construction holds up under scrutiny, but thirty wards sit close enough to Ward 5's number that a two point band would sweep in nearly the entire group. This same measure crowds nearly the whole city into a four point range, so finishing worst here mostly means sitting inside a pack rather than standing apart at the very bottom.
writeup.summary:
Ward 5 spans Woodlawn, Hyde Park, South Shore, and Greater Grand Crossing along Chicago's South Side lakefront. Its 47.95 score is good for 20th place among the fifty. Environmental readings carry the ward's strongest marks. Modeled exposure to air pollution, distance from major polluting facilities, and the annual count of demolition permits all place this ward first citywide.

New construction tells the opposite story. Residential building permits are scarce, and new housing construction has nearly stalled. Nightlife is thin too, with few bars turning up per resident, and chains account for a bigger slice of local restaurants than in most of the fifty. The overall picture is a quiet, mostly residential ward that scores well on the environment and light on new building.

writeup.headline: Ward 6 lands 44th of 50, with the city's highest reported violent crime rate.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Start with the worst number. Ward 6's violent crime rate runs about 709 incidents per 10,000 residents, the highest reading among the 50 wards. The count starts with census tracts, each one split evenly across its area regardless of where people actually cluster inside it, and then laid onto the ward map, so a tract only partly inside Ward 6 still contributes its full share here. Confidence in the number is only medium, by the compiler's own admission. Two of Ward 6's best numbers deserve a similar gut check. Its first-place ranks on modeled religious attendance and modeled daily leisure time are not measurements taken inside the ward at all. They're a profile, built from national survey data, describing what places sharing this area's demographic mix tend to look like elsewhere, not a local count of anyone's actual habits here. The people behind the model rate it low confidence, for both figures alike. Ward 6's first-place rank on the parks share of aldermanic menu money is a real number, but it comes with its own asterisk. Boundaries moved in 2023, and part of what's being counted here may still carry the ward's old shape rather than its current one. On top of that, some wards are simply missing from this one entirely, so the citywide comparison isn't running on the same footing for everyone.
writeup.summary:
Ward 6 covers Greater Grand Crossing, Chatham, Englewood, and Roseland on Chicago's South Side. Of the fifty wards, it lands 44th. That rank comes from a composite score of 32.14, in the lower half of the citywide range.

The ward's clearest strengths are in retail character and city administration. Just 1.54 percent of its licensed food stores belong to one of the 100 largest retail chains, the lowest share in Chicago, and its building permits move through the city faster than in nearly every other ward. Safety and demographics pull the other way. Ward 6 carries the highest reported violent crime rate of the 50 wards, the lowest share of multilingual households, and one of the thinnest counts of sit-down restaurants per resident. Most of its food retail stays independent of the big chains, even as crime and language diversity remain real weak points.

writeup.headline: South Chicago and South Shore anchor a ward with the fewest restaurants in the city.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Start with traffic proximity, where Ward 7 ranks 1st of 50 on the city's Environmental Justice Index. Behind the No. 1 rank sits the same tract-splitting method used across that index. Each census tract's traffic exposure is divided evenly across its acreage and then handed to whichever ward covers that ground, so a tract straddling the Ward 7 line contributes to both sides at once, regardless of where the traffic actually runs. Confidence here again lands at medium, per whoever assembled the index. The restaurant count, dead last at 50th, has a different problem. It is not a ward number at all. It gets built from ZIP code areas, which cut across ward lines however they happen to fall, with no attempt to match the two. This one is rated low confidence too, straight from the people who compiled it. Packaged liquor licenses and food business counts, also dead last, trace back to a ward field the source recorded before the 2023 redraw, so some of what's being measured still reflects the old ward shape rather than today's.
writeup.summary:
Ward 7 sits on Chicago's far southeast side, taking in South Deering, South Chicago, South Shore, and Calumet Heights. Only two wards score lower than Ward 7's 48th-place finish. Its combined score sits at 29.04, among the lowest of the fifty.

Commercial life is where the ward struggles most. Ward 7 finishes last in the city, 50th of 50, on restaurants, on food businesses of any kind, and on places still open past 9 p.m. on a weeknight. Commute times are the longest in Chicago too, with about 41 percent of workers on the road 45 minutes or more each way. Rent runs the other direction. Among the 48 wards with reliable rent data, Ward 7 lands 3rd, with a typical asking rent of $1,463, one of the cheapest anywhere in the city. A cluster of pollution-exposure measures also score well for Ward 7, though each comes with its own caveat, covered below.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the No. 1 rank in child care centers per resident first. That childcare count is drawn from ZIP code areas instead of ward boundaries, and the two maps don't line up anywhere in the city. Low confidence is attached to this figure too. The last-place rank in coffee shops looks just as stark, until you read the caveat underneath it. Two points also separates Ward 9's last-place coffee-shop count from eleven other wards, so the bottom of this particular ranking sits closer together than the single rank position suggests. Its source treats every acre of a census tract as if the same number of people lived on it, an assumption that breaks down wherever a tract crosses into the next ward. writeup.summary:
Roseland, West Pullman, Riverdale, and Pullman make up Ward 9 on Chicago's Far South Side. Its overall standing is 43rd out of the fifty. A score of 32.29 sits behind that number, below the citywide average.

Family life and faith drive its strongest numbers. Ward 9 has the highest count of child care centers per resident in Chicago, its 311 pothole requests close in about two and a half days on average, the second-fastest turnaround citywide, and mapped houses of worship are denser here than almost anywhere else in the fifty. Commuting and nightlife pull the numbers down. Two in five workers here report a commute of 45 minutes or longer, among the longest stretches in Chicago. The ward has almost no bars or coffee shops by the count used in this report, and it posts the worst reading in the city on a wastewater-proximity index built from environmental justice data. Ward 9 reads as a place organized around home, family, and worship, with little built around nightlife or a short commute.

writeup.headline: Cheapest rent and most park land in Ward 10 pair with the city's lowest income.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the No. 1 rank for rent first. Both the census survey and a real-time listing index put Ward 10 at the cheapest in the city, and that part holds up as a real signal. That census figure gets divided across tracts using their area rather than by where renters actually live, so a tract that crosses into a neighboring ward still contributes its full, evenly divided share to Ward 10's number. The bottom-of-the-list rank on household income tells a thinner story. That figure comes from income data covering several wards at once, so a cluster of neighboring wards ends up with close to the same score by construction, not because of anything specific happening inside Ward 10 itself. The last-place rank for gathering spots like bars, cafes, and gyms sits somewhere in between the two. Two points is the entire gap between Ward 10's count and five other wards, so the rank makes this ward look like more of an outlier than the numbers really support.
writeup.summary:
South Deering, Hegewisch, East Side, and part of Riverdale form Ward 10 on the Far Southeast Side. Thirty-two wards score higher than Ward 10, putting it 33rd overall. Its composite score comes to 37.43, roughly in the middle of the pack.

Physical space and cost of living are its clearest strengths. Ward 10 has the most park acreage per resident of the fifty wards, the lowest measured rent in Chicago on both a census survey and real-time listing data, and the lightest air-toxics burden citywide on the environmental justice index used here. The weaker numbers involve crowding and cash income rather than pollution or space. Ward 10 has the lowest count of bars, cafes, gyms, and other gathering spots per resident citywide, and its measured household income sits at the bottom of the list. Off-street parking lots are scarce too. Ward 10 reads as a place with room to breathe and comparatively cheap housing, set against thin nightlife options and comparatively low measured income.

writeup.headline: Fastest streetlight fixes in the city pair with heavy industrial exposure in Ward 11.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two figures here deserve a second look before they carry full weight. The 1st-place mark on streetlight repair time, 1.48 days on average, is real, though this particular count isn't tracked in every one of Chicago's fifty wards, so fewer than fifty are actually being compared. The last-place mark on proximity to hazardous risk management plan sites carries more caveats. Confidence on this particular figure is graded medium by the agency that publishes it, and the number was carved up by acreage, not by a household count, so a tract that straddles the ward line hands part of its total to the neighbors. Most of the fifty aren't far apart here either, the middle twenty-five wards on this measure span just eleven points, so last place is not necessarily far from fortieth. The chain-restaurant figure, 1st place at only six percent of the ward's restaurants tied to a major chain, carries none of those caveats and holds up without qualification.
writeup.summary:
No ward in Chicago closes a broken streetlight request faster than Ward 11, averaging 1.48 days. That speed helps push the ward to 13th of 50 overall, solidly in the top third of the city. Ward 11 sits on the Near South Side and covers Bridgeport, Armour Square, New City, and McKinley Park. Restaurants skew independent too, with a smaller share of chain outlets than anywhere else in Chicago, and grocery access ranks second best citywide.

Ward 11's problems cluster around industry. It sits last among the fifty on proximity to sites with hazardous-chemical risk management plans, and lags most of Chicago on nearby major-emitter facilities, diesel particulate matter in the air, and traffic exposure near homes. All four measures point toward heavier industrial exposure than the rest of Chicago sees.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: A couple of these figures deserve a closer look. Ward 12's second-place score on participatory budgeting looks close to the top, but the field crowding that score runs thirteen wards deep before it drops two points, so second and several wards below it aren't meaningfully far apart. The 49th-place mark on mental health providers, 0.9 per 10,000 residents, looks close to the worst in Chicago, but the crowd stuck near that same low score runs twenty-two wards deep before it climbs two points. The middle fifty percent of wards on this measure crowd into a narrow seven-point band too, so a lot of the city sits close to that same low mark, and Ward 12's rank comes from landing inside that band. The park fountain lead figure carries none of that hedging. Two out of three of the ward's tested fountains came back flagged, and the source attaches no caveat to that number.
writeup.summary:
Three in four households in Ward 12 speak something other than English at home, the third-highest share in Chicago. That's one piece of a ward sitting at 31st of 50 overall, in the lower half of the city. Ward 12 covers Brighton Park, McKinley Park, New City, and the Lower West Side on the Southwest Side. The ward also carries one of the lowest shares of people living alone in Chicago, and it ranks second on participatory budgeting, meaning residents get a direct vote on how the ward's menu money gets spent.

The weaker numbers touch health access and everyday gathering spots. Ward 12 has the second-lowest count of mental health providers per resident in Chicago, and sits behind most of Chicago on third places, the cafes, bars, restaurants, and gyms where people spend informal time. Recorded real estate sales run low too, and the ward used only about 70 percent of its yearly aldermanic menu budget in the most recent full year, one of the lower utilization rates in Chicago. The starkest number sits at the park level, where Ward 12 sits in last place, 50th of 50, on the share of park fountains carrying a historically elevated lead reading.

writeup.headline: Ward 13 finishes 26th of 50, quick on city services, thin on housing reinvestment.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: A few of these numbers deserve a second look. Ward 13's third-place score on menu money spent, all of its roughly $1.5 million in yearly aldermanic capital funds committed, sounds decisive, but the pack scored right behind it runs sixteen wards deep before the score drops two points, so third and, say, tenth aren't meaningfully different. The second-place mark on demolition permits, just one issued in the tracked year, looks just as strong, but the agency behind the number rates its own confidence here as medium, and it isn't tracked the same way in every ward, so a single unfiled or reclassified permit could move the number. The ward's last-place score on fine-particulate air pollution comes from two separate sources, and both split their readings across ward lines by surface area instead of tallying up households block by block, so some of what's measured here may really belong to a neighboring ward.
writeup.summary:
Broken garbage cart requests get closed faster in Ward 13 than anywhere else the city tracks, at 17.81 days on average. That habit belongs to a ward parked at 26th of 50 overall, right around the midpoint of the rankings. Ward 13 covers Clearing, Garfield Ridge, West Lawn and West Elsdon on the Southwest Side, near Midway Airport. Only two wards commit more of their yearly aldermanic menu money to actual projects instead of leaving it unspent, and the ward gets more direct sunlight at street level than almost any other ward, both across the year and on the summer solstice.

The weak spots sit in housing and air quality. Ward 13 comes in last of the fifty on dollars invested in residential renovation permits, and last on the size of its surveyed stock of historic buildings built before 1940. Two separate measures of fine-particle air pollution both put it last, and it sits well back of the city average on worship-related activity and the number of cafes, bars, restaurants and other everyday gathering spots per resident. Taken together, this is a settled, well-serviced residential ward that isn't drawing much new housing investment or many informal places to gather.

writeup.headline: Language diversity sets Ward 14 apart, though housing investment lags far behind.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of these figures need a closer look. The top rank on language, roughly eighty-five percent of residents reporting a home language besides English, comes from a direct Census Bureau count rather than a model, though the total still gets divided by how much land each tract covers, not by how many households sit inside it, so homes near the edge of Ward 14 could actually be counted toward a different ward's tally. The second-place mark on modeled no-religious-affiliation share looks just as solid, since a low modeled share counts as a strong score on this measure, but the two numbers come from different places entirely. A national survey pushed down to ward level produced this estimate, not a headcount taken inside Ward 14, and the group that built it calls the number low confidence. The last-place rank on religious congregations rests on ZIP code data, and ZIP codes don't follow ward boundaries at all, so this number may really describe a differently drawn area than Ward 14 itself.
writeup.summary:
About eighty-five percent of Ward 14 residents use a language other than English inside the home, the highest rate of the fifty wards. That share comes from a ward stuck at 41st of 50 overall, deep in the bottom fifth of the rankings. Ward 14 covers Archer Heights, Gage Park, Chicago Lawn and Brighton Park on the Southwest Side. It also has the second-lowest share of people living alone, so more households here share a home than in nearly every other ward, and a modeled estimate puts it among the more religious wards, with the share of residents expected to report no religious affiliation running lower than in nearly all fifty. Median rent for renters paying cash rent is the third-lowest in the city, and ozone pollution is lower here than in all but four other wards.

The weak spots are investment and a handful of less common measures. Ward 14 sits last of the fifty on residential renovation permits issued, and last on the dollar value of recorded property sales in the latest year. It also carries the lowest density of massage and bodywork businesses in the city, and sits closer than anywhere else in Chicago to facilities that report toxic releases. Congregation counts trail the same way, with the fewest religious congregations carrying paid staff per resident anywhere in the fifty. Together, these numbers describe a linguistically diverse, family-dense residential ward with comparatively low housing turnover and more exposure to industrial sites than most of Chicago.

writeup.headline: Gage Park anchors Ward 15, independent on business, weak on civic turnout.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of the ward's strongest marks come from business licensing data. Local restaurants and grocers dominate the count, with chain restaurant share ranked 2nd of 50 at 19.05 percent of licensed restaurants, and major chain store share ranked 2nd as well, at 1.79 percent of licensed food stores. Both figures are tied to the ward boundary as it stood when the license was recorded, and before 2023 this was a differently shaped ward, so some of the older records describe a boundary that no longer exists. The agency behind this data puts its own confidence at medium, not high, and the licensing tally behind both measures doesn't reach every one of the fifty wards either. The ward also ranks 2nd on non-routine bills sponsored by alders associated with it this council session, 206 in total, a count of legislative activity tied to the ward rather than a measure of any one official's output. That number carries the same before-2023 boundary caveat as the business data. On the softer end, the ward ranks 49th of 50 on the modeled share of adults who talk or spend time with neighbors at least monthly, which this dataset puts at 0 percent. This figure comes from a model built on a national survey and pushed down to the ward level, not from anyone actually counting conversations on the block, and the group behind the estimate calls its own confidence low. So the number says more about how Ward 15 compares to the other forty-nine than about any specific count of actual conversations.
writeup.summary:
Independent restaurants and grocers dominate here in Ward 15, with chain restaurant share ranking 2nd of 50 citywide at just over 19 percent of licensed restaurants. This pairing sits inside a ward that finishes 42nd of 50 overall, well below the city's midpoint. Ward 15 stretches across New City, Gage Park, West Englewood, and Chicago Lawn on the Southwest Side. Coffee shops here also rate among the best in Chicago, and voter turnout runs low, with just over 22 percent of registered voters casting ballots in the most recent municipal election, one of the lower turnout rates in the city.

Ride-share spending and recorded real estate sales both sit near the bottom of the fifty wards, and residents report some of the lowest rates of physical activity and everyday contact with neighbors anywhere in Chicago.

writeup.headline: Ward 16 ranks last of the fifty overall, though its permits and fountains lead the city.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Building permits here average zero days to issue, the fastest processing in the city. That ranking runs against just 47 of the fifty wards, since three don't have enough recorded permits for the source to judge, and the agency behind the number calls the figure medium confidence. A zero-day average likely reflects a small handful of recorded permits rather than a permit office outrunning the rest of Chicago.

The park fountain figure carries no caveat at all. None of the sites tested in the ward by Should I Drink Here? returned a historically elevated lead reading, the cleanest result of the fifty wards in the comparison.

The weakest number comes from the CDC's PLACES program, which puts 34.9 percent of adults here at fair or poor general health, the highest share in the city. That estimate is built by dividing census-tract totals across the ward using land area as the yardstick, treating every corner of a tract as equally populated, so wherever a tract sits across the ward line, part of what's counted here really belongs next door. Confidence in the number sits at medium, per the same agency.
writeup.summary:
Englewood, West Englewood, Chicago Lawn and New City make up Ward 16 on Chicago's South Side. Its overall score, 25.3, is the lowest in the report, placing Ward 16 last of the fifty.

A few measures move against that trend. Building permits here process faster than anywhere else the source could rate, and none of the Park District fountains tested in the ward turned up an elevated lead reading. Asking rents also sit among the lowest in the city. Health numbers pull the overall score down hard. Ward 16 posts the worst share of adults reporting fair or poor general health in the city, the highest rate of physical inactivity anywhere in Chicago, and the lowest voter turnout of the fifty wards.

writeup.headline: Six citywide last-place rankings weigh down Ward 17's 45th-of-50 overall finish.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
The 2nd-place finish on time poverty looks like a clear win, but the number behind it is a prediction about the ward rather than something measured in it. It comes from a model built on national survey patterns, not a survey taken here, and its confidence rating from the source is low.

The worst-in-the-city rank on mental health providers is a real count, 0.62 providers per 10,000 residents. Move the score here two points, though, and 22 other wards swap places with it. A 7-point spread covers the middle of the field on this measure, so most of the wards near the bottom sit close together, and the ranking is sharper than the gap behind it.

Civic engagement, also ranked 50th, is built from census-tract totals divided onto the ward by geography. Part of what gets counted in a border tract really sits in the neighboring ward instead of this one, and the agency that compiles it rates the number low confidence.
writeup.summary:
Ward 17 covers Auburn Gresham, West Englewood, Chicago Lawn and Englewood on Chicago's South Side, and lands 45th of the fifty in the overall ranking. Several of its numbers rank among the best in Chicago. Council session attendance for the seat sits 2nd in the city, at 97 percent. The ward also counts 96 mapped houses of worship, second-most of the fifty, and ranks 2nd for worship places measured per resident. A modeled estimate of time poverty, the share of residents getting under two hours of daily leisure, puts Ward 17 2nd at 17.7 percent. Pothole repairs close in about four days on average, third-fastest citywide, and park acreage per resident ranks 3rd.

The weaker numbers are more numerous, and more extreme. Ward 17 finishes last in the city, 50th of the fifty, on six separate measures. Those are civic engagement, the share of adults sleeping under seven hours a night, mental health providers per resident, licensed restaurants that serve liquor, chronic school absenteeism, and the share of workers who walk or bike to work. Parks, churches and fast pothole repairs sit right alongside some of the roughest numbers in the city for health access, sleep, schooling and civic life.

writeup.reading_the_rankings:
The last-place rank on grocery stores sounds decisive, but the group publishing it calls the measure medium confidence, and its coverage isn't complete for every ward. Some of what looks like Ward 18 falling behind might just be the record catching up elsewhere.

The 4th-place rank for spending the aldermanic capital budget looks strong next to a full 100 percent utilization. Nudge that score two points either way, though, and sixteen wards trade spots with it. Most of the city spends nearly all of what it's allotted, so a top-four finish here is closer to keeping pace than standing out.

Rent burden, also last in the city at 63 percent, comes from Census figures apportioned onto ward lines using tract geography rather than a block-by-block count. That means a chunk of what's attributed to Ward 18 on this measure may actually belong to whichever ward sits on the other side of that tract line. Medium confidence, by the agency's own rating.
writeup.summary:
Ashburn, Auburn Gresham, West Lawn and Chicago Lawn make up Ward 18 on Chicago's Southwest Side, which ranks 35th of the fifty overall, closer to the middle than either extreme. Its strongest marks describe the physical stock of the place. writeup.headline: Voter turnout in Ward 19 is highest in the city, even as its grocery access ranks lowest.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Ward 19's rank of first for voter turnout is a straight count, 62 percent of registered voters cast a ballot, well ahead of every other ward. That count is tallied against the ward's current boundaries. The 2023 remap redrew these lines, so an election held under the old, differently shaped ward isn't directly comparable.

Its rank of 50th, dead last, on menu spending diversity looks damning next to that voter-turnout number, but the caveat attached to the measure argues the opposite. It only tracks how spread out the aldermanic infrastructure budget is across project types, and concentrating money in one category isn't described as better or worse than spreading it around.

A rank of 49th on entertainment venues carries a similar twist. Shift that score two points and sixteen wards jump ahead of or behind this one. The whole city also crowds into a 10-point range on this measure, so a rank in the high 40s reflects a small gap in a crowded field rather than real distance from the rest of the city.
writeup.summary:
Beverly, Mount Greenwood, Morgan Park and Auburn Gresham form Ward 19 on the far southwest side, ranked 7th of the fifty overall, one of the higher scores in the report. The strongest numbers include the smallest measured exposure to hazardous-waste facilities of the fifty wards, the highest share of aldermanic menu money put toward street resurfacing, 99.6 percent, and the highest voter turnout in the city, 62 percent of registered voters. A separate set of top scores are predictions about the ward's residents rather than observations of them, modeled from survey patterns on resident satisfaction and safety rather than a poll taken here.

The weaker numbers describe a different kind of place. Ward 19 has the fewest grocery stores per resident anywhere in the city, just over one per 10,000 people, and ranks among the weakest in Chicago for licensed entertainment venues, fine-particulate air pollution and ride-share spending. Just 9.2 percent of workers here commute by public transit, third lowest of the fifty. Together, the numbers describe a mostly residential part of the city built more around driving than transit or retail.

writeup.headline: Poverty runs highest in Ward 20, even as parking and paving numbers rank among the best.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Ward 20's worst score, a poverty-rate rank of 50th at 34.7 percent, comes from an actual Census count, not a model, divided among wards using each tract's land area as the basis, so part of what's tallied here may really sit next door. Whoever compiles that reallocation calls it only medium confidence, since census tracts and ward boundaries don't line up neatly.

Three other bottom-ranked measures sit right behind it. Financial satisfaction, social trust and happiness are all predictions about the ward rather than observations of it, built from national survey patterns and the ward's demographic makeup rather than a poll of anyone who lives here. The agency rates all three low confidence.

The ward's fifth-place rank on permit-zone parking density is a different case, a number with no caveats attached at all, about as close as this report gets to a figure that means exactly what it says.
writeup.summary:
New City, Washington Park, Woodlawn and Englewood share Ward 20 on the South Side, which finishes fifth from last of the fifty overall. Poverty is the clearest weak point. At 34.7 percent, the share of residents below the poverty line is the highest of the fifty wards, and median household income lands near the low end of the fifty too, at about $40,500 a year. Three modeled wellbeing measures, happiness, financial satisfaction and social trust, land at or near last place as well, though those come from estimates built on population traits rather than a survey of the people who actually live here.

The ward's other numbers tell a different story. It lands in the top five of the fifty on the share of menu money spent on street resurfacing and on how many parking permit zones cover its blocks, and in the top ten on new residential building permits, 22 issued over the past year. Together, the numbers show a ward carrying real material hardship on one side and steady infrastructure and construction activity on the other.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: Three of Ward 21's six best rankings track religious attendance, and all three come from one demographic model rather than a survey conducted here. Wards with a population mix like this one turn up nearly identical numbers by construction, and the estimate carries a low confidence rating from its source, so the weekly-attendance and strongly-religious figures describe a modeled pattern, not a count of who showed up on a given Sunday. The alley-repair and spending-diversity rankings near the bottom are the flip side of that street-paving strength. With 97 percent of menu money going to streets, little was left for alleys or anything else, which is why both land in the mid-40s citywide. The liquor-license ranking, 49th in the city, looks worse than the gap behind it. Twelve wards are effectively tied with Ward 21 here, the whole group sitting inside a two-point spread.
writeup.summary:
Ward 21 covers Washington Heights, West Pullman, Morgan Park, and Roseland on Chicago's Far South Side. It comes in 34th citywide, with a combined score of 37.04. A caveat attaches to most of what gets measured here, 164 of the 181 rankings this ward has on record.

The strongest numbers cluster around schools and streets. Per-pupil school spending ranks 2nd citywide, and just over 97 percent of the ward's aldermanic menu money went toward resurfacing streets, a top-3 share in Chicago. The weak spots sit on the retail and nightlife side. Ward 21 has the highest share of chain restaurants in the city, no bars rated 4.5 stars or better with at least 50 reviews, and almost no restaurants licensed to serve liquor. That combination points to a residential ward where schools and street paving are the visible public investment, not a built-out commercial strip.

writeup.headline: Share of one-person households ranks lowest citywide, while park space ranks last here.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: A few of these numbers are softer than they look. That last-place finish comes with an asterisk. Thirty-six wards cluster together on the measure labeled review count, value 1,070, none more than two points apart, which turns the whole stretch into an effective tie rather than a real last place. Between the thirteenth-best ward and the thirty-eighth on that same measure there are only two points, so most of the fifty land close to the middle no matter where the number falls. Two of the strengths are modeled estimates rather than counts of anything that happened here. The 3rd-place rank for adults with no religious affiliation, 19.4 percent, and the last-place rank for adults expected to visit a bar weekly, 4.1 percent, both come from survey-based statistical models. Wards with similar demographics tend to produce close to the same modeled number by construction, and this one is flagged low confidence by whoever built it. Read both as a general pattern built from the area's makeup, not a figure gathered from Ward 23 residents directly.
writeup.summary:
Garfield Ridge, West Lawn, West Elsdon, and Archer Heights fall inside Ward 23, on Chicago's Southwest Side. It comes in 32nd citywide, with a score of 39.76, below the midpoint of the fifty but well clear of the bottom. Its strongest measures point to a tightly knit residential area. Share of one-person households ranks lowest in Chicago here, meaning shared and family households are more common than in any other ward. Licensed tobacco retailers per resident rank 2nd, so only one ward has fewer of them for the people it holds, and landlord profit on rental units ranks 3rd on two separate measures, meaning renters here keep more of what they pay than in most of the city.

Where the ward falls short is public and gathering space. It ranks last in Chicago for parks, with just 4 mapped inside its boundaries, for civic and cultural places (18 of them), and for houses of worship per resident. It also ranks last for cars per household, with the highest average number of vehicles per home in the city, and last for the modeled share of adults expected to visit a bar weekly. Put together, the picture is a residential, car-dependent stretch of the Southwest Side with little built infrastructure for public life outside the home.

writeup.headline: Grocery access and school funding rank first, environmental burden ranks worst here.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: A few of these numbers deserve a second look before they settle anything. The 1st-place rank for grocery stores per resident comes from a source that counts businesses by ZIP code, and ZIP codes were drawn for a different purpose than ward maps, so the two do not line up. Some of that count may really sit inside a neighboring ward instead. The last-place rank on the Environmental Justice Index runs into a version of the same problem, only with census tracts standing in for ZIP codes, and tracts don't follow ward lines any more neatly than ZIP codes do. Where a tract crosses the boundary, part of that score may end up credited to the ward next door. The last-place rank for social trust, 19 percent, comes from a statistical model built from citywide survey and demographic data. That estimate comes tagged low confidence, and it describes a pattern typical of wards built like this one on average, not something collected from Ward 24 residents directly.
writeup.summary:
West Side neighborhoods North Lawndale, South Lawndale, Austin, and West Garfield Park make up Ward 24. It sits 47th citywide, with a score of 29.61, well down the list. Its strongest measures cluster around schools, food access, and neighborhood institutions. The ward ranks 1st in Chicago for mapped faith institutions, with 101 of them, and 1st for houses of worship per resident. It also ranks 1st for grocery stores and supermarkets per resident and 1st for per-pupil school spending, at $23,663 per student. Two modeled estimates land near the top as well, for daily leisure time and for how often residents are expected to spend an evening with neighbors.

The weaker numbers point to environmental and social strain. The ward ranks last in Chicago on the Chicago Environmental Justice Index, the city's measure of cumulative pollution and vulnerability where a higher score means a heavier burden, and last on the related share of residents living in an EJ-designated area. It also ranks last for modeled social trust, for the share of adults reporting frequent mental distress, for how connected people say they feel to their neighborhood, and for highly rated bars, of which the ward has zero. Together, the numbers describe a ward where schools and neighborhood institutions rank strong while the surrounding environment and public-health measures rank among the worst in the city.

writeup.headline: Ward 25 comes in 28th citywide, clean air paired with heavy pollution-burden scores.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the environmental numbers first. Ozone ranks 1st citywide, the lowest average ground-level ozone reading anywhere in Chicago. Pollution burden and proximity to major industrial emitters land 47th and 48th. All three come from the same city environmental justice index, and that index carries a medium confidence tag. It also draws on census tracts, laid out for a different purpose than ward boundaries and never quite matching them, so a slice of any tract's numbers can end up credited to the ward next door. Ozone measures one narrow thing, ambient gas levels in the air. Pollution burden and facility proximity measure something else, how close people live to major polluters. A ward can land at the top on one and near the bottom on the other, and that is what happened here. Participatory budgeting ranks 3rd. All of the ward's menu money is governed by resident vote. But thirteen wards land close enough to call it a wash, all inside a two-point band, so third place reads more like a wide tie than a clear lead. The ward's last-place rank on trust in local government rests on a number not every ward supplies, so the ranking reflects only the wards that reported one, maybe fewer than fifty.
writeup.summary:
Pilsen, Little Village, and slices of the Near West Side and North Lawndale make up Ward 25. It lands 28th citywide, a score of 44.71 that puts it in the middle of the pack. The strongest numbers here are about money and food. The ward puts more of its aldermanic menu budget into alley repair and school projects than almost anywhere else in Chicago. Residents also get a direct vote on that same menu spending. Grocery access and coffee shop ratings both rank in the top three citywide.

The weak spots are environmental and educational. Trust in local government here lands at the very bottom of the fifty. Two pollution measures from the city's environmental justice index also land 47th and 48th, well down the list, even though the ward's ozone reading is the best in the city. Chronic school absenteeism is among the highest citywide, and licensed child care per resident is thin. Pilsen and Little Village both sit close against the industrial corridor along the Chicago River, and the ward's environmental numbers move in different directions depending on which specific measure you look at.

writeup.headline: Independent restaurants outnumber chains here, but pothole repairs rank slowest citywide.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of the weakest rankings are really the same story told twice. Pothole repair time and general 311 response time both come from the city's 311 system, and coverage gaps mean fewer than fifty wards have logged enough requests to make the comparison complete, so each ranking reflects whichever wards have enough data to sit in it, not a full match-up against every ward. Menu budget utilization tells a different kind of story. The ward spent 85.3 percent of its roughly $1.5 million annual menu allotment, which reads like solid follow-through, but that number lands only 44th, because most other wards spent an even higher share of theirs. And the ward's best ranking, the lowest chain-restaurant share in Chicago, rests on a business-license snapshot tied to a ward boundary recorded at the time it was pulled. Chicago redrew its ward lines in 2023, so a comparison against that older boundary is shaky, and whoever compiled the figure graded their own confidence in it medium, not high.
writeup.summary:
Ward 26 covers Humboldt Park, West Town, Logan Square, and Hermosa. A composite score of 46.83 places it 22nd out of 50, just above the citywide middle. The ward carries the lowest share of chain restaurants of the fifty and the second-lowest share of chain food stores, and its bars post some of the highest average ratings in Chicago. Aldermanic menu spending here is also the most geographically spread out of the fifty, reaching a wide range of blocks rather than clustering in one spot.

The clearest weakness is how fast the city responds once something breaks. Pothole repair time is the slowest of the fifty, over 60 days on average, and general 311 response time is second slowest, just over 16 days. Yoga and pilates studios are effectively absent, 48th of 50, and school proficiency lands at 43rd.

writeup.headline: Ward 27 leads Chicago on new housing investment and trails it on pollution-site proximity.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The attendance figure that puts the ward at 50th of 50, 41 percent, comes from a count that folds together more than one term in office. The measure's own description explains that whenever representation changed mid-session, the source combines whoever held the seat across the full year into one ward number, so the 41 percent reflects the ward's full-year record rather than any single person's time in the chair. The three first-place construction rankings, spanning investment dollars, permit count, and estimated new units, read as commanding, but the central half of the ranking is only about four to five points wide on those measures, so most wards in Chicago sit close together and Ward 27's lead is a narrow margin over a crowded field rather than a wide one. The TIF increment ranking, also first in the city at $256.4 million, rests on the softest evidence of the group. The team behind that figure rates it low confidence by their own admission, and the field behind it runs one ward short of the complete fifty.
writeup.summary:
Near West Side, West Town, Humboldt Park, and Near North Side make up Ward 27. Its composite score of 50.61 puts it 15th out of 50, in the upper half of the city. New construction is most of the story here. The ward leads the city in reported investment in new residential permits, at $279.7 million, in the number of new permits issued, 44, and in the estimated new housing units those permits will bring, 633. It also collected more TIF increment revenue than anywhere else in Chicago, $256.4 million, and every graffiti removal request logged here closed in zero days, also a citywide best. Arts and culture ranks second, with 13 mapped venues and spaces.

The weaknesses sit somewhere else. Ward 27 posts the worst pollution-site proximity score in the city, a measure of how close residents live to Superfund sites, brownfields, and other contaminated land under state remediation. It also sits low on both traffic injuries and pedestrian and cyclist crashes, each 49th of 50. Licensed music and dance venues are scarce too, last among the 48 wards with usable data.

writeup.headline: 902 traffic injuries last year is the most in Chicago, even as Ward 28 leads on gardens.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The third and fourth-place ranks on how often residents see friends and neighbors weekly, 18.3 percent and 20.7 percent, read like real community strength, but neither number is measured inside Ward 28 at all. Both come out of a model built on age, income, and household make-up in wards with similar demographics and density, not anything counted on these blocks, and whoever built the estimate calls it low confidence too. The 50th-place rank on traffic injuries, 902 people hurt in police-reported crashes last year, is a more literal count, though that category's field comes up short of the full fifty, since not every ward logs enough crash data to be compared. The poverty rate, 48th of 50 at 30.5 percent, is an area-weighted number. It comes from splitting each census tract by how much of its area sits inside the ward line, then counting the tract's population toward whichever ward holds the bigger slice. Wherever a tract straddles the boundary, some of that 30.5 percent really belongs next door.
writeup.summary:
Ward 28 stretches across Near West Side, East Garfield Park, West Garfield Park, and Austin, with a composite score of 36.54 that puts it 36th out of 50, below the citywide midpoint. The ward has more mapped gardens than anywhere else in the city, 23 in total, and ranks fourth on the count of civic, cultural, and public places, with 136 mapped. It also ranks fourth on the share of aldermanic menu money spent resurfacing alleys, at 44.7 percent, and fourth on new residential permits issued, 29 in total. Modeled estimates put the ward third in the city on how often residents socialize with neighbors weekly, 18.3 percent, and fourth on seeing friends weekly, 20.7 percent, though both figures come from a statistical model rather than a survey of the ward itself.

The weak spots cluster around safety and cost of living. Ward 28 recorded 902 traffic injuries last year, the highest count of the fifty. Close to half of its licensed restaurants, 49.2 percent, are chain outlets rather than independents, near the foot of that ranking citywide. Almost a third of residents, 30.5 percent, live below the poverty line, 48th of 50, and the ward also posts weak numbers on faith diversity among houses of worship and on two separate readings of pollution exposure, both tied to Superfund and brownfield sites and other contaminated land nearby.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the camera-spending share, which ranks 2nd out of 50 at 0.2 percent of the ward's menu money. The middle band of that scale is under a single point wide citywide, so nearly the whole city sits at a similarly low share, and a rank of 2 says less than it looks like. The wastewater proximity score, a measure of industrial pollution near local streams, ranks 3rd out of 50, but a two-point slice of that scale holds thirty-five wards, and this ward is one of them, so the ranking here reads sharper than the real gap behind it. The estimate itself comes from working out how big a piece of each nearby tract sits inside the 29th's boundary, so a wedge of a bordering tract's number can land here even though the ward does not reach that tract directly. The garden count runs the other way. It ranks 47th with zero gardens mapped, but a two-point band on that scale holds eighteen wards, including this one, so the sharp-looking rank sits on top of a fairly small real gap.
writeup.summary:
Ward 29 sits on Chicago's West Side, taking in Austin, Montclare, Dunning, and Belmont Cragin. Its composite score of 35.2 lands it 38th out of 50, in the bottom third of the city. Air quality and a quick-moving 311 system are what stand out first. Chicago 311 closes graffiti requests here almost immediately, and the ward posts the lowest average ozone reading of the fifty on one air-quality measure, with a similarly strong showing on a second, separate measure that ranks seventh.

Outdoor space and upkeep are where the numbers turn weaker. Mapped gardens, registered murals, and distance to the lake all sit near the foot of the list, half of the ward's park drinking fountains have tested positive for elevated lead at some point, and pothole repairs run slower here than almost anywhere else in the city.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of these numbers ride on the city's aldermanic menu-money records, and those got redrawn right along with the ward lines in 2023. writeup.summary:
Portage Park, Belmont Cragin, Irving Park, and Avondale fall inside Ward 30, on Chicago's Northwest Side. A composite score of 45.96 lands it 24th out of 50, close to the middle of the city. writeup.headline: Belmont Cragin's ward leads on polluted-site exposure, trails on new housing.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Take the top ranking on polluted-site proximity. It looks like a clean sweep, but confidence is not high here, by the source's own grading, and a few wards never reported this measure at all, so the comparison sits on a thinner field than the full fifty.

Ward 31's last-place finish on new homes permitted looks like an outlier, but it barely is. Twenty-nine other wards sit less than two points off its score, and citywide, most wards land somewhere inside a five-point band on this measure, so the bottom of this list is really most of Chicago packed into one narrow stretch.

The menu-spending rankings carry a different asterisk. These lines are only a couple of years old, redrawn in 2023, so some of the historical spending behind the fifth-place mark on spending spread and the sixth-place mark on sidewalk spending was actually recorded against a differently shaped ward.
writeup.summary:
Belmont Cragin, Hermosa, Portage Park and Avondale make up Ward 31 on the Northwest Side. An overall score of 36.09 puts the ward 37th among the fifty, under the midpoint of the city. It holds the smallest measured exposure to polluted sites of the fifty wards, and 71.7 percent of its households speak a language other than English at home, the fourth highest share in Chicago. Aldermanic menu money here spreads across a wide run of blocks rather than bunching in one corner, city crews close street light outages in an average of 1.68 days, among the fastest turnarounds anywhere in the city, and about 26.7 percent of households have a householder living alone, ranking eighth of the fifty on that measure.

The weaker numbers cluster around housing and health coverage. An estimated 18.3 percent of residents have no health insurance, the highest uninsured share in the city. Parking disputes and complaints also run higher here than anywhere else in Chicago, across both measures the ward tracks, and builders pulled only one new residential permit last year, the fewest citywide. Rodent baiting requests take longer to close here than in any other ward. Ward 31 pairs clean industrial-site numbers and fast city response on basic requests with a housing supply that has nearly stopped growing.

writeup.headline: Ward 32 ranks second of 50, led by income, thin on neighbor socializing.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
A few of these numbers carry real fine print. Take the modeled happiness ranking. The estimate was assembled rather than collected, built from the ward's income, marital status, employment, homeownership and health mix, not a survey of residents here, and the source's own grading puts confidence on this one at the low end, so it reflects the ward's demographic mix more than how people here actually feel day to day.

The bars-and-taverns ranking rests on different ground. It comes from ZIP code data that does not follow ward lines at all, so some of what counts toward Ward 32's first-place mark may sit in a neighboring ward, or miss a bar that falls just across a ZIP boundary.

The near-bottom finish on mapped landmarks looks worse than the real gap behind it. Twenty wards cluster within a couple of points of Ward 32's mark, and this measure squeezes nearly the whole city into a 6.2-point span, so a landmark count pulled from OpenStreetMap is bunching most of Chicago near the same low mark, not singling out this ward.
writeup.summary:
Logan Square, Lincoln Park, North Center and Lake View combine into a North Side ward defined by money and modeled well-being, one that finishes 2nd overall in the city, its score of 63.81 trailing only one other ward. Median household income here is $166,248, the highest reading anywhere in the city, and the poverty rate sits at 5.9 percent, the lowest such rate in Chicago. A model built from income, employment, marital status, homeownership and health also puts the ward first on both subjective happiness and the modeled share of adults who would call themselves very happy. The ward also carries the most bars and taverns per resident in Chicago and ranks first on the population-vulnerability piece of the city's environmental justice index, a socioeconomic and health-risk score built from census data.

The weaker numbers point to time and social connection more than money. A model of daily routines puts the ward last of 50 on both minutes of daily leisure and the modeled share of adults who socialize with neighbors weekly, and 49th of 50 on time poverty. The ward also recorded 38 demolition permits, more than anywhere else in Chicago, and this dataset's map of landmarks and community gardens turns up none inside Ward 32, each ranking 49th of 50. Ward 32 is a wealthy, busy ward where residents report less unstructured time and fewer casual neighborhood ties than the rest of the city.

writeup.headline: 13.79 percent of Ward 33's licensed food stores are chains, the lowest share in the city.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
A couple of these numbers need their caveats attached. Ward 33's lowest chain-store share in the city, just under 14 percent, is pulled from a business-license field tied to the ward as it stood whenever each license was filed. The ward's boundaries changed in 2023, recently enough that some of the older licenses behind that number describe a differently shaped ward than the one that exists now. The same recent redraw sits behind the last-place finish on menu money spent, where only 55.9 percent of the ward's roughly $1.5 million annual allotment went to committed projects in the latest full year.

The near-last finish on total place reviews reads harsher than the real numbers support. Thirty-six of the fifty wards come in less than two points apart from Ward 33 on this measure, and citywide this measure barely spans two points from top to bottom, so the rank here is sharper than the gap it is actually measuring.
writeup.summary:
Albany Park, Irving Park, Avondale and North Park sit inside a ward whose strongest marks come from neighborhood life rather than city government, one that lands squarely in the city's middle, 25th overall out of fifty, scoring 45.91. The ward's bars carry a median Google rating of 4.75, the best score among the 45 wards with rated bars, and its houses of worship rate close behind at 4.9. Places across the ward rate second-best in the city overall, at 4.73 out of 5. Chain outlets make up just under 14 percent of the ward's licensed food stores, the smallest share in Chicago, with the rest independently owned. The ward also reports fewer traffic-crash injuries than all but two others citywide, and ranks third for how many home languages are spoken there, a mark tied to Albany Park's long history as a landing spot for immigrant and refugee families.

The weak points are almost all city services, not neighborhood character. Ward 33 lands 48th of 50 on both 311 response time and pothole repair time, and dead last, 50th of 50, on the share of its yearly menu money actually spent on projects instead of left idle. The ward has no libraries mapped inside its boundaries either, also last in the city. Registered murals rank 48th of 49, and total place reviews rank 49th of 50. Ward 33 pairs an active bar and worship scene and mostly independent local businesses with a ward that trails most of the city on infrastructure and how fast basic requests get handled.

writeup.headline: Bank branches per resident put Ward 34 first, landlord profit share puts it last.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Two of Ward 34's numbers deserve a second look before taking them at face value. Its last-place finish on landlord profit share, above 69 percent under both the assessed-value and sale-price versions of the estimate, sounds like an outlier at first glance. Ten other wards land inside a two-point margin of that same mark on each version of the estimate, so the ward sits at the extreme end of a citywide pattern rather than standing apart from it. The sale-price version in particular is flagged by its own source as likely to read thin or even negative for anyone who bought recently, since it swaps in a mortgage basis closer to what current owners actually paid.

On the strong side, the first-place marks for bank branches, coffee shops, and gyms per resident come from a source that spreads county-level business counts across ZIP code areas rather than ward lines, and by that source's own scale, confidence here sits on the low side too, so a true ward-by-ward count could look different.
writeup.summary:
The Loop, Near West Side, Near South Side and West Town form the dense center of downtown Chicago, a business-and-transit hub that finishes 8th overall citywide, scoring 55.86. Every one of its strongest marks comes in first in the city. It has more bank branches per resident than anywhere else in Chicago, nearly 24 per 10,000 residents, and it also leads the city on coffee shops, gyms, and religious congregations, each counted per resident. It also logs the most 'L' station entries among wards with rail service, more than 7.4 million rides recorded at stations inside its boundaries. Licensed coffee and tea shops per resident rank first as well. Ward 34 is built around density and heavy daytime foot traffic more than a typical residential neighborhood.

The weak points cluster around cost of living rather than city services. Ward 34 finishes last in the city on the estimated share of rent that ends up as landlord profit, above 69 percent whether the estimate uses assessed property values or actual recent sale prices. It also finishes last on a modeled estimate of the share of adults with no religious affiliation, on licensed tobacco retailers per resident, and on the share of licensed food stores that belong to a major national chain. None of Ward 34's six weakest measures are 311 response time, pothole repair, or library and park counts, the city-service categories that sit at the bottom in many other wards.

writeup.headline: Independent restaurants define Ward 35's strength, thin park acreage its clearest gap.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Park Access lands at 48th out of 50, but that ranking is softer than it looks. A dozen other wards come within a similarly tight band of Ward 35's score, and this measure's citywide range runs a full eleven points, wider than most of the ward-level numbers here, so the real distance between Ward 35 and much of Chicago is smaller than 48th place implies.

The fourth-place rank on menu money spent on bike and pedestrian projects is tied to the ward's footprint as it stands today, redrawn in 2023, so it reads as one year's snapshot, not a running trend for a single continuous ward.

And the attendance figure, in the bottom five for the ward's representation, blends more than one alderman's term across that same 2023 boundary change, and it carries only medium confidence in the source's own grading.
writeup.summary:
Avondale, Logan Square, Irving Park and Hermosa sit inside a Northwest Side ward built around independent restaurants and bike-friendly spending, one that finishes 14th overall out of fifty, on a score of 51.1. Its restaurants skew independent rather than chain, the second-lowest chain share of the fifty, and its bars post some of the highest average ratings in the city. City infrastructure money backs that pattern up. The ward has put a larger share of its aldermanic menu funds into bike lanes, sidewalks, and street redesigns than all but three wards, and it spreads that money across more kinds of projects than most wards do.

The ward falls behind on green space and a couple of slower-moving city services. Park acreage per resident is among the lowest in the city, and only two wards are slower to close a rodent baiting request. Estimated adult loneliness runs higher than most of Chicago too, and the ward's dense permit parking zones point to a real parking squeeze. Council attendance tied to the ward's representation lands in the bottom five, though that figure blends more than one alderman's term across the 2023 boundary change. Ward 35 reads as a walkable stretch of the city with a strong restaurant and bar scene and real money going into biking and walking routes, even where green space and a couple of routine services have not kept pace.

writeup.headline: Strong bar and worship ratings sit alongside a shortfall in park space in Ward 36.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Ward 36's top spot on bills sponsored carries an asterisk. Chicago redrew ward boundaries in 2023, so the count reflects today's district lines more than one alderman's full term in the seat, and the underlying data only carries a medium-confidence label. Fifth place on the city's traffic proximity index tells a similar story from a different angle. That figure gets assigned by area from census tracts rather than measured block by block, so some of what shows up here really belongs to the wards next door, and the rank also reads sharper than it is, since fourteen other wards land inside two points of this one. Forty-fifth for mental health providers per resident looks worse than the real gap behind it. Only two points separate Ward 36 from twenty-five other wards on this measure, and the typical spread across the middle of the city here runs to just seven points, so most wards, whatever their overall rank, look a lot alike on this one.
writeup.summary:
Belmont Cragin, West Town, Montclare, and Humboldt Park make up Ward 36, on Chicago's Northwest Side. The ward sits 27th among the city's 50 wards, scoring 45.79 out of 100. Two of its top scores trace back to city government activity. It leads every ward in Chicago on bills sponsored, a count of non-routine legislation tied to this council session, and it also tops the city on the cut of infrastructure menu money spent on alley repair. Its houses of worship post some of the highest ratings anywhere in Chicago, and its bars score among the best in the city.

The softer numbers cluster around green space, health access, and street friction. Park acreage per resident sits well below most of the city, mental health providers per resident are scarce next to most wards, and parking complaints run higher here than almost anywhere in Chicago. Demolition permits and mapped landmarks also land in the bottom ten. Put together, this is a dense stretch of the city with strong food, drink, and worship options, next to real gaps in park space and mental health access.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: A few of these numbers need a caveat attached. writeup.summary:
Second from the bottom of Chicago's 50 wards, Ward 37 takes in Austin, Humboldt Park, Belmont Cragin, and West Garfield Park on the West Side. Its combined score lands it 49th of 50 citywide. That low number splits into two different pictures. A handful of measures here beat almost every other ward, while most of the rest land dead last.

The strongest results are how quickly the city closes graffiti requests, the ward's ozone reading, and the share of its infrastructure budget spent on sidewalk repair, each placing in the top five citywide. The weakest results all land in last place, and there are six of them. They cover diversity of religious traditions among local houses of worship, a modeled measure of social cohesion, school proficiency, a modeled estimate of how many adults work with neighbors on something for the community, licensed bars and taverns, and bank branches per resident.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: A few of these numbers carry real qualifiers. First place is less about distance from the pack than it looks, since a full thirty-four wards match this score within two points on the pollution-proximity measure. writeup.summary:
Ward 38 covers Dunning, O'Hare, Portage Park, and part of Belmont Cragin on Chicago's Far Northwest Side. It lands 18th of Chicago's 50 wards on the overall measure, solidly in the upper half of the city. Its strongest numbers touch civic spending and how connected residents feel to their neighbors. Its clearest weak spot is how residents get around town.

The ward posts the best score in Chicago on a measure of pollution near local waterways, and again on schools, the biggest single category in its infrastructure menu spending. It also ranks second for its estimated rate of adult loneliness, one of the lowest readings in Chicago, and second on the ward's trust in local government score. The weak spot is public transit. Only 7.7 percent of workers here commute by bus or train, the lowest share anywhere in Chicago, and the ward also lags on lakefront distance, on a modeled figure, not a headcount, for how often adults see friends, and on how little of its menu budget went to alley repairs.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: A couple of these numbers deserve a second look. Alder attendance for the current council session lands third of 50, which sounds strong, but part of this record predates the 2023 remap, so the figure blends today's ward lines with whoever held the seat before boundaries changed, and the source marks the underlying number medium confidence. Park spending from the aldermanic menu fund also lands third, though the caveat here is different. On this measure, the typical middle-of-the-city range is barely a third of a point wide, so a small shift in dollars can jump a ward several spots. The weaker rankings carry their own caveat too. The estimate that only 16.6 percent of residents see friends weekly comes from a model built on national survey data and the ward's own demographics. Nothing here was counted door to door, and the source flags it low confidence besides.
writeup.summary:
Libraries are Ward 39's standout, with the second highest count anywhere in Chicago. Its houses of worship also span one of the widest ranges of religious traditions in the city. Add faster than typical building permits and a larger than typical share of aldermanic menu money spent on parks, and the ward's civic numbers read strong across the board. All of that lands Ward 39 12th of 50 wards overall, solidly in the top third of the city. It covers North Park, Forest Glen, Albany Park, and Irving Park, on the city's Northwest Side.

The weak points sit in schools and in the kind of places that bring people together outside their own block. Per-pupil school spending sits at the very bottom of the fifty wards. Licensed music and dance venues are among the scarcest in the city, and a modeled estimate, not a headcount, puts the share of residents seeing friends weekly well below most other wards. Over half the ward's park water fountains also carry a history of elevated lead readings, a bigger share than in almost any other ward. Together, the numbers describe a ward that is steady on the basics of city government but thin on nightlife and casual social contact.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: A couple of these rankings are softer than they look. Resident metric ideas submitted to Ward Wise Explorer put the ward 46th of 50, which reads like low civic engagement on its face, but two points is all that separates this ward from thirty-nine others here, and the middle band of all fifty wards on this question spans nothing at all, essentially zero points. How much of Ward 40's menu dollars went toward relighting streets and alleys is the next number worth a caveat. That measure lands the ward 44th of 50, but the gap is mostly noise. Only two points keep this ranking apart from thirty-eight others in the city. This figure also carries a 2023 boundary redraw in its history, meaning older years counted a differently shaped ward. It also only exists for some of the fifty, since a handful of wards never reported a figure here at all. A rank this low barely separates Ward 40 from most of the city. writeup.summary:
8.75 micrograms per cubic meter, Ward 40's fine-particle pollution reading, is among the lowest anywhere in Chicago. The ward covers Lincoln Square, West Ridge, Edgewater, and Rogers Park on the North Side, and lands 16th of 50 wards overall, just inside the city's top third. This is a ward that beats most of Chicago on some kinds of air pollution but falls behind on food access and school funding.
