writeup.headline: Norwood Park and Edison Park sit in Ward 41, Chicago's sunniest, most lake-distant ward.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Start with the violent crime number, where Ward 41 comes in lowest of the fifty. That figure leans on a stand-in for population. Crime counts get split across ward lines by each census tract's land area, not by where people actually live inside it, so a tract that straddles two wards can hand some of a neighbor's crime total to Ward 41's side of the ledger, or the reverse. The last-place rank on seeing friends weekly is softer still. It is not a headcount. It borrows its behavior pattern from a national sample of adults who share Ward 41's rough demographic profile, and the group behind it grades the result low confidence on its own scale. The bottom rank on Divvy rides has the opposite shape. Count down twenty-seven wards from Ward 41 on this measure, and the score has still not dropped two points, because a full eleven points of spread holds half of the wards in this measure. Last place sits inside a thick cluster rather than standing apart from it.
writeup.summary:
Ohare, Norwood Park, Edison Park and Jefferson Park make up Ward 41, sitting in tenth place out of Chicago's fifty wards, inside the top fifth of the field. Its strongest numbers are physical. Ground-level spots here get more direct sunlight across the year than anywhere else in Chicago, true on the summer solstice and the winter one alike. The ward also logs the fewest abandoned-vehicle and bike-lane parking complaints per square kilometer anywhere in the city, and its reported violent crime rate comes in lowest on this data set.

The softer numbers trace back to distance. A modeled estimate of how often adults spend an evening with friends weekly puts Ward 41 last of the fifty, and public transit use for commuting lands 49th. Divvy ridership and straight-line distance from the lake round out the bottom of the list too. Ward 41 sits at the city's far edge, away from downtown and the lakefront, which explains a good share of those softer numbers.

writeup.headline: Highest income in Chicago pairs with the highest rent and the least sunlight in Ward 42.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Start with average income, the ward's headline number. It comes from IRS tax data apportioned across ZIP code boundaries that never lined up with ward lines to begin with, so what lands on Ward 42 really describes the ZIP codes touching it more than the ward itself. The people who publish that figure grade it low confidence, and a chunk of the fifty wards are missing the number entirely. The rent number carries a smaller version of the same problem. It gets divided among wards using each census tract's land area as a proxy for where renters actually live, so a tract that crosses into a cheaper neighboring ward can pull Ward 42's number in either direction. The child care rank has a different catch. It sits on a ward boundary recorded at the time the source counted it, and Chicago redrew those boundaries in 2023, so part of what this number reflects belongs to a ward shape that no longer exists on the map.
writeup.summary:
Ward 42 covers the Loop, the Near North Side, West Town, and part of the Near West Side, the downtown core and the blocks immediately around it. It holds down fifth place out of the city's fifty wards. Its strengths cluster around downtown living. More residents here commute on foot or by bike than anywhere else in the city, and the ward has more mapped arts and culture spots than anywhere else in Chicago. Average income reported on tax returns filed from the ward is the highest in Chicago, and city crews close out 311 requests here faster than anywhere else, both for potholes and for rodent complaints.

The weak points line up with density and shadow. Downtown's tall buildings block a lot of direct sunlight at street level, and the ward finishes last in the city for ground-level sun access on both solstices. Pedestrian and cyclist crash counts and median rent both come in last too, and licensed child care per resident is lower here than anywhere else in Chicago. Ward 42 combines the city's top income and arts numbers with its highest rent and dimmest streets.

writeup.headline: Ward 43 ranks first of 50, strong on history and ties, weak on street lights.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the historic buildings count, where Ward 43 leads with 1,531 structures logged in the city's historic resources survey. That survey never reached every ward on equal footing, so wards missing a full count drop out of this particular comparison, and a lower rank elsewhere might just mean a corner of the city the survey covered less thoroughly, not one with less history. The street light repair ranking cuts the other way. Ward 43 finishes last at 3.16 days to close a request, and the same gap in coverage applies here too, so a faster time in another ward may reflect a more complete record rather than quicker crews. The depression ranking, where Ward 43 also finishes last, has the thinnest paper trail of any number in this report. The underlying data file carries no listed source and no description for it, on top of the usual gaps in ward coverage, which is reason enough to treat that single ranking as a question for further reporting rather than a settled fact.
writeup.summary:
Lincoln Park, the Near North Side, and Lake View make up Ward 43, which finishes at the very top of the fifty-ward field this year. That comes with an overall score of 66.01. Most of the lead traces to history and social connection. The ward holds more buildings logged in the city's 1983 to 1995 historic resources survey than anywhere else in Chicago, and it takes the top spot on several measures of how connected and supported residents feel, plus the highest concentration of licensed music and dance venues and the lowest rate of elevated childhood lead levels.

The rest of the picture is less even. Ward 43 finishes last of the fifty on how quickly the city repairs a broken street light, and last on a measure tied to depression rates. It also scores low on parking availability and per-pupil school spending.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: Park space is the clearest case. Ward 44 finishes last at 0.73 acres per 10,000 residents, but half of Chicago's fifty wards land inside an eleven-point band on this measure, so last place mainly means a crowded bottom, not a rare gap. Worship engagement, counted from Google reviews of local religious buildings, puts Ward 44 last too, though that number tracks who has claimed an online listing more than who actually attends. A thin count here could just mean fewer nearby congregations have gotten around to a page. The four religion measures behind that, covering weekly attendance, strength of belief, and certainty about God, all rank Ward 44 last as well. None of those four numbers come from asking anyone in Ward 44 a question. Each one is stitched together from how people nationwide with a similar mix of age, income and household type tend to answer, and every one of those four carries the same low confidence grade from its source.
writeup.summary:
Lake View and part of Lincoln Park make up Ward 44. Citywide, it sits sixth out of fifty wards this year, with an overall score of 60.13. Top marks cluster around city responsiveness and a dense bar and tavern scene. The ward finishes first on how fast the city closes routine 311 requests, first on the city's environmental justice index, and first on both the count of highly rated bars and the rate of licensed taverns per resident. Street and alley lighting soaked up more of Ward 44's aldermanic menu budget than any other project category last year, 41.6 percent of the total.

The weaker measures land in two areas, park space and religion. Ward 44 finishes last of all fifty wards on park acres per resident and last on a measure of reviews for local worship spaces. It also finishes last on several modeled estimates of religious belief and attendance, projections built from national survey data rather than a local count of who attends services.

writeup.headline: Zero percent of Ward 45's menu money went to sidewalks, even with strong safety numbers.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the loneliness figure first, where Ward 45 posts the lowest rate in the city. It comes from spreading a census survey across each tract by land area rather than by actual population, so a slice of the number may really belong to a neighboring ward, and its own confidence grade comes in low. The violent crime rank, second-best citywide, rests on that same tract-by-area method, and here the source marks it only medium confidence. The ward's 49th of 50 finish on participatory budgeting looks worse on paper than it plays out in practice. Walk down the list from Ward 45's spot at 49th and you can cross off thirty-seven wards before the score moves two points, because most of Chicago never set up a participatory budgeting vote to begin with.
writeup.summary:
Jefferson Park, Forest Glen, Portage Park and Norwood Park make up Ward 45, on the Northwest Side, landing ninth in the citywide count of fifty. Residents here report some of the lowest loneliness rates anywhere in Chicago. The ward also comes in second-lowest on violent crime and third-best on feeling safe walking alone at night. It put nearly all of its menu money into street resurfacing last year, behind only one other ward.

Everything else in Ward 45 runs thinner. The ward spent none of its menu money on sidewalks or on bike and pedestrian projects, and it runs no participatory budgeting process for residents to vote on how that money gets spent, though most Chicago wards skip that too. Response time on rodent baiting requests and the property tax dollars captured by TIF districts also sit close to the bottom of the list.

writeup.headline: 49 registered murals top Chicago, but Ward 46 has the city's slowest cart repairs.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
The mural count only tallies wards where the Chicago Mural Registry has data on file, so Ward 46's total of 49 is a lead among however many wards were actually measured, not a guarantee it would win against a full field of fifty.

The freight-rail figure comes from cutting citywide pollution data into ward-sized pieces by area rather than counting anyone directly, a method that can hand a slice of a neighboring ward's exposure to this one, and it carries only a medium confidence rating from the source that built it.

Ward 46's near-last finish on museums, 49th of 50, sits inside a crowd. Twenty-two other wards also land on that same zero, so a near-last finish here means good company more than a real gap.
writeup.summary:
Freight rail runs farther from Ward 46 than from any other ward in Chicago, and industrial toxic-release sites sit almost as distant, the second-lowest exposure in the city. Uptown and a slice of Lake View make up the ward, which lands 19th of 50 overall with a score of 48.1, not far from the midpoint of the fifty. It also holds the most registered murals of any ward measured, 49 in total, and posts the second-highest share of residents who commute by public transit, just over 32 percent.

The bottom of the list looks different. No house of worship in the ward carries a rating of 4.8 or higher with at least 25 reviews, and last year none of its menu money went to bike or pedestrian projects. Garbage cart repair requests take about a month to close here, longer than anywhere else in the city, and only 9.6 percent of menu spending went to street resurfacing, among the smallest shares of the fifty.

writeup.headline: Ward 47 ranks third of 50, leads on schools and broadband, trails on groceries.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Ward 47's top rank on feeling part of the neighborhood reads like an easy win, but the survey behind it carries a low confidence rating from its own source, and the numbers get spread across census tracts that do not line up neatly with the ward's actual boundaries.

Its rank of 49th for lighting dollars sits inside a genuine pile-up. At the bottom of this particular list, a two-point gap barely counts as one, and thirty-eight wards crowd into that same narrow stretch. On this measure half of Chicago's fifty wards fit inside a span of just two points, tight enough that a small budget shift could reorder the whole bottom of the table.

The ward also lands 49th of 50 on per-pupil school spending even while it ranks 1st on the share of students meeting state proficiency standards, two figures the data never claims to connect.
writeup.summary:
Broadband reaches 94.9 percent of Ward 47's households, the highest connection rate in Chicago. The ward covers North Center, Lincoln Square, Lake View and Uptown, and its overall score of 63.64 lands it 3rd of 50 wards, just outside the top two. It also leads the city on a survey measure of feeling part of the neighborhood, on licensed child care centers per resident, and on the share of students at nearby schools meeting state proficiency standards. Its aldermanic menu spending spreads across a wide mix of project categories too, the second most balanced mix of any ward.

Retail and public spending pull the numbers down. The ward sits 49th of 50 for licensed grocery stores per resident and last but one in the city for its menu dollars spent on lighting for streets and alleys. It also trails on demolition permits issued, well below most of the fifty, and on a modeled share of residents getting less than two hours of daily leisure time. Ward 47 reads as a well-connected, high-performing stretch of the North Side that comes up short on grocery retail and on where its public lighting dollars go.

writeup.headline: Edgewater anchors Ward 48, the closest of the fifty wards to Lake Michigan's shore.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
Ward 48's last-place finish on worship ratings comes from a median Google score of 4.7, still a strong rating in absolute terms, and twelve other wards sit close enough to call it a virtual tie, so last place here reads more like a rounding matter than a real shortfall.

Its 49th-place rank on park spending sits inside an even bigger cluster, forty wards deep, where two points hardly separate anyone. The middle two-quarters of Chicago's wards squeeze into a band just three tenths of a point wide on this particular measure, so almost the whole city occupies the same narrow spot and the order could flip on pocket change.

Even the ward's first-place rank on civic engagement carries a footnote. It comes from a ZIP-code stand-in for volunteering, and it too arrives with a low confidence rating attached from the source, since Chicago's ZIP boundaries don't line up with its ward lines.
writeup.summary:
Ward 48 sits closer to Lake Michigan than the other forty-nine wards, averaging about half a mile to the shoreline. Its score of 47.91 puts it 21st out of 50, close to the city's midpoint, across Edgewater, Uptown and Rogers Park. Its aldermanic menu spending splits across a wider mix of project types than any other ward. It also posts the top score in Chicago on civic engagement and on how many different faiths its houses of worship represent, and ranks second-best on fine-particle air quality.

The softer numbers cluster around modeled safety and where capital dollars go. None of Ward 48's menu dollars went to street and alley lighting last year, the only ward in Chicago at zero on that count, which lands it dead last of the fifty. Park spending sits almost as low, 49th of 50. The ward also ranks 49th on a modeled estimate of adults afraid to walk alone at night, and just over half its households have someone living alone, among the highest shares in the city. Ward 48 pairs some of the best lakefront access in Chicago with softer numbers on solitude, night-time safety perception, and where its public dollars go for lighting and parks.

writeup.headline: Lowest fine-particle pollution in the city lands in Ward 49, where ozone ranks worst.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
The fine-particle numbers rate Ward 49 first in the city on four separate air and pollution measures, but the source that built them calls its own confidence level medium, and the underlying data is not filled in for every ward, so a first-place finish here describes the wards actually measured rather than a guaranteed sweep of the full fifty.

Ozone lands at the opposite end of the table, last place, and that is not a contradiction. Ozone and fine particles come from different sources and behave differently once they are airborne, so a ward can top one list and trail the other on air quality alone.

The modeled fear-of-walking figure, also last place, is not a crime count or a neighborhood survey. It is a statistical estimate built from national data, the kind of model that holds up well in aggregate across many places but is a weak read on any single ward, and the source attaches a low confidence rating to it.
writeup.summary:
Fine-particle pollution measures lowest in Ward 49 of any ward in Chicago, alongside the lowest diesel exhaust and the lowest industrial toxic-release levels, the top rank in the city on three separate environmental-justice measures. The ward covers Rogers Park, West Ridge, and Edgewater on the city's northern lakefront, and its overall score of 42.78 lands it 30th of 50, a little below the midpoint of the rankings. It also recorded the fewest traffic injuries anywhere in Chicago last year, 87, and put a larger share of its menu money into bike lanes, sidewalks, and street redesign than any other ward, 47.9 percent, well above the usual mix of paving and parking work.

The weak spots sit somewhere else. Ozone measures worst in the city, the opposite result from the fine-particle numbers above, because ozone and fine particles are different pollutants that form and travel differently through the air. Two modeled measures also land at the very bottom of the fifty, the share of adults who feel unsafe going out alone after dark and the share reporting loneliness. The ward spent none of its menu money on alley repair, and its rate of abandoned-vehicle and bike-lane parking complaints trails every ward except one.

writeup.headline: Most grocery stores per resident, zero participatory budgeting, both describe Ward 50.
writeup.reading_the_rankings:
The grocery-store ranking carries an asterisk. Ward boundaries changed in the 2023 redraw, so this count reflects today's ward rather than the one on older maps, and the business-license data behind it earns only a medium confidence mark from the agency that compiles it, with gaps in some other wards.

The worship rankings look just as strong on paper, first place both for top-rated congregations and for total review volume, but on the review measure specifically, the middle fifty percent of Chicago's wards are packed into a window just 6.8 points wide, so finishing first here is a narrow win, not a runaway one.

On the other end, Ward 50's last-place score on participatory budgeting sits beside thirty-seven other wards posting that same zero, and the practice barely exists anywhere in the city yet. That ranking says more about Chicago's habits than about this one ward specifically.
writeup.summary:
More licensed grocery stores serve Ward 50's residents than any other ward in Chicago, 8.7 per 10,000 people. The ward covers West Ridge, North Park, Lincoln Square, and part of Rogers Park in the city's far north, along the Devon Avenue corridor, and its score of 46.43 places it 23rd of 50, just above the midpoint. Its strongest marks otherwise are about daily life. The ward also has the widest mix of home languages spoken of any ward, and the most highly rated houses of worship in the city, both by count of top-rated congregations and by how many reviews they draw.

Civic participation and recreation options pull the score down. The ward has no yoga or pilates studios and no mapped museums, and it logged zero resident-submitted ideas to the Ward Wise Explorer metric project. It also runs no participatory budgeting process, where residents would get a direct vote on some menu-money spending, and none of its reported menu money went specifically to school or park improvements. Dozens of other wards report the identical zero on most of these counts, so finishing last here usually means sharing the bottom rather than standing alone.
